frame: A waterproof logbook has washed up on Hollowgum's beach. The Squintle won't stop staring at it.
text: Research ship Southern Petrel, Day 4. At 0600 we lowered the submersible, which the crew calls the Tin Can, into the trench off Cape Brindle. Dr Okafor piloted, and I sat beside her with the cameras, trying not to think about the two kilometres of water waiting below us. The Tin Can is about the size of a family car, and it smells of cold coffee and nervous people. At 800 metres the last trace of sunlight vanished, and the only light came from tiny glowing creatures drifting past like sparks. At 1,400 metres we spotted our first target: a ghost shark, pale and silvery, with eyes like dinner plates. It circled us twice before disappearing into the gloom. The real surprise came at 1,900 metres, where the sea floor was carpeted with thousands of purple sea cucumbers, all slowly vacuuming the mud. Some were as long as my arm. Dr Okafor laughed so hard she fogged up the window. We collected three samples with the robotic arm, although one sea cucumber defended itself by squirting its sticky insides all over the claw. We began our ascent at 1130 and surfaced at 1340, starving and slightly seasick. Tomorrow we dive again, this time hoping to find the giant sea louse that was filmed here in 1998.

frame: Zed has posted a game review on the ship's noticeboard. Check what it really says.
text: REVIEW: LANTERN DRIFT, by Zed. Lantern Drift is a puzzle game in which you guide a paper lantern down a river at night, lighting up hidden paths for a lost fox cub. Each level adds something new, such as whirlpools, sleeping owls or floating ice. There are forty levels, and each one takes about five minutes, although the final level took me nearly an hour and two packets of crackers. The controls are simple: tilt the screen to steer, and tap to make the lantern glow brighter. Glowing brighter uses up oil, so you have to decide when the extra light is worth it. The fox cub follows close behind and gives a tiny yip whenever it finds a star. The music is gentle and plinky, which I liked at first but found slightly annoying by level thirty. The best feature is the photo mode, which lets you pause anywhere and snap the scenery, and I have taken about three hundred shots of the same waterfall. My only real complaint is that you can't replay a level once you have finished it, so if you miss a hidden star, it's gone for good. Overall, Lantern Drift is calm, clever and occasionally frustrating. I give it eight lanterns out of ten.

SANDCASTLE CHAMPIONSHIP GOES AHEAD DESPITE WARNINGS

Organisers of the Hollowgum Sandcastle Championship have refused to move tomorrow's event, even though the weather service has issued a king tide warning for the entire coast. The championship begins at 1 pm on the flat stretch of sand below Gull Point, where competitors will have exactly three hours to build. More than sixty teams are expected, and the castles will be judged at the end of the three hours. According to the tide chart pinned up at the surf club, high tide will arrive at 3:40 pm, and it is expected to be the highest tide of the year. Locals say that even during an ordinary high tide, the water reaches the bottom of the Gull Point stairs, and Gull Point is the lowest part of the beach. Some families have asked for the start to be moved to the morning, when the tide is out. Last year's champion, eleven-year-old Archie Tran, said he wasn't worried. "I'm building a moat this year," he said. "A really deep one." Head organiser Bev Saddler insists the event is perfectly safe. "The judges will be sitting up on the dunes," she said, "so they'll have a lovely view of the whole beach." Meanwhile, the surf club has quietly moved its rescue boards and flags to the top of the car park.

UPDATE, 4:30 pm: The king tide came in far lower than the weather service forecast. It stopped twenty metres short of the first castle, and Archie's moat stayed completely dry. The weather service says a change in the wind held the water back.

text: The Hollowgum Bakery had spent months planning its attempt to bake the world's largest lamington. The official measurement was booked for midday on Saturday in the town square. Unfortunately, Saturday turned out to be the hottest day of the year. Some children were spotted eating the fallen coconut straight off the cobblestones. Rather than give up, head baker Rosa Liu grabbed a microphone and asked the crowd for help. Within an hour, locals had carried over buckets of custard, jelly and cream from their kitchens, and the bakers layered it all, melted lamington included, into an empty paddling pool. The judge measured the result and confirmed it as the world's largest trifle, a record nobody had ever attempted before. The bakery says it will try the lamington again, this time in winter. frame: Indi brought home a gallery guide. The Glowerbill is checking which artworks could really be in the show.
text: The sculptor Mira Okoye has one strict rule: she never buys a single material. Every piece in her new exhibition, Tideline, was made from rubbish she collected on the beaches of Hollowgum Island over two years. She walks the high-tide mark every morning with a sack, picking up bottle caps, thongs, rope, broken toys and tangled fishing line. Okoye also refuses to use glue, nails or screws, so each sculpture is held together with knots of washed-up fishing line, some of them so tiny that she ties them with tweezers. Nor will she paint anything. Every colour in the exhibition is exactly as the sea left it, which is why so many of her animals are faded blues, sun-bleached pinks and the dull green of old nets. Some pieces are enormous, like a whale skeleton three metres long built from washed-up white plastic pipes. Others are tiny, like a family of ants made from scraps of coloured net. Okoye says her rules are the point of the work, because they force visitors to notice how much plastic washes up on a single island. The exhibition runs until the end of March, and entry is free. Visitors are asked not to touch, because the knots can loosen. Children can join a beach clean-up with the artist every Saturday morning.
